issues.legal_issue: The constitutional protection for laws acquiring, extinguishing, or modifying rights in an estate does not extend to a law that transfers a holder’s property to family members without changing the land-tenure relationships associated with the estate.
material_facts: The respondents relied on the constitutional protection for laws affecting estates and the petitioner’s properties were assumed, for deciding that argument, to be held in janmam right.
The challenged law deemed qualifying sthanams to be tarwads and their properties to belong to the tarwads, thereby giving the tarwad members rights in property previously held by the sthanee.
The law did not regulate relations between landlords and tenants, change the incidents of janmam rights, or implement agrarian reform; it transferred property interests between family members.
issues.conclusion: The challenged law did not fall within the constitutional protection for laws affecting estates and could not, on that ground, avoid review under the fundamental rights guarantees.
issues.legal_principle: The majority construed the estate-related protection as addressing acquisition of an estate or modification or extinguishment of rights pertaining to land tenure, including relations between landlords and subordinate tenure-holders. It relied on Aswini Kumar Ghose v. Arabinda Bose for the limited use of legislative objects and reasons to identify the circumstances and purpose of a constitutional amendment, and distinguished Sri Ram Ram Narain v. State of Bombay and Atma Ram v. State of Punjab as cases involving legislation regulating land-tenure rights and agrarian reform. Justices Imam and Sarkar dissented, reading the protection more broadly to cover modification of a holder’s rights by transferring them to joint holders.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_property_law: A party challenged the constitutionality of a law that affected property rights.
predicates.law_transfers_estate_property_between_fa: The law transferred property held by one family member to other family members or made them joint holders.
predicates.law_changes_land_tenure_relations: The law altered land-tenure rights or relationships, such as the rights between a landholder and subordinate tenure-holders.

issues.definition: When a challenged law transfers estate property between family members without changing land-tenure relations, the estate-related protection does not bar review of the law under fundamental rights guarantees.

issues.legal_issue: A law depriving a person of property is not insulated from other fundamental rights guarantees merely because it operates under authority of law.
material_facts: The respondents argued that the property deprivation authorized by the challenged law was governed exclusively by the constitutional provision concerning deprivation of property and therefore did not have to satisfy the guarantee of the right to hold and dispose of property.
The constitutional amendment had separated compulsory acquisition and requisition from other forms of deprivation of property.
The majority found that the challenged law deprived the sthanee of property, and that the estate-related protection did not apply.
issues.conclusion: The authority-of-law requirement did not exclude review under the property-rights guarantee; a property-deprivation law had to comply with the applicable fundamental rights guarantees unless a specific constitutional exception applied.
issues.legal_principle: The majority held that a law must be within the legislature’s competence and must not infringe fundamental rights, subject to applicable constitutional exceptions. It relied on Deep Chand v. State of Uttar Pradesh and Basheshar Nath v. Commissioner of Income-tax for the limits imposed on legislation by the Constitution and fundamental rights. It distinguished A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras because the relevant personal-liberty provisions formed a different constitutional scheme, and held State of Bombay v. Bhanji Munji inapplicable after the constitutional amendment separating acquisition and requisition from other deprivation. It also considered State of West Bengal v. Subodh Gopal Bose and referred to Narendra Kumar v. Union of India on the possibility that even a prohibition may qualify as a restriction if reasonable.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_property_dep: A party challenged a law that deprived a person of property on constitutional grounds.
predicates.constitutional_text_separates_acquisitio: The constitutional scheme treats compulsory acquisition or requisition as distinct from other forms of deprivation of property.
predicates.law_deprives_person_of_property: The law takes property from a person or materially removes that person’s property interest.

issues.definition: When a challenged law deprives a person of property under a constitutional scheme that distinguishes acquisition from other deprivation, the law remains subject to review under the other applicable fundamental rights guarantees.

issues.legal_issue: A law that uses criteria unrelated to the legal character of property to transfer it from its holder to others is an unreasonable restriction on the holder’s property rights when the transfer is not justified in the interests of the general public.
material_facts: The challenged law treated a sthanam as a tarwad, and its properties as tarwad properties, if there had been intermingling of the properties, maintenance of tarwad members from sthanam property, or a vacancy in succession to the sthanam.

Under the Marumakkathayam law described by the Court, a sthanee had no present proprietary interest in tarwad property, and tarwad members had no present proprietary interest in sthanam property; their possible rights were contingent succession rights.

The Court held that intermingling, maintenance payments, and a temporary absence of an eligible male successor did not establish that sthanam property had become tarwad property under the applicable law.
The challenged law operated retrospectively, affected titles established by court decisions, and transferred property interests without compensation.
The record did not establish that the transfer served the general public or answered a real and genuine grievance.
issues.conclusion: The challenged law infringed the property-rights guarantee and was not saved as a reasonable restriction in the interests of the general public; the majority declared the law void and ultra vires.
issues.legal_principle: A restriction must be non-arbitrary, reasonably related to its object, and in the interests of the general public; its reasonableness depends on the circumstances of the case. The majority relied on State of Madras v. V.G. Row for the factors relevant to reasonableness, and on Narendra Kumar v. Union of India for the proposition that even a prohibition may be a restriction but requires strict scrutiny. It applied the Marumakkathayam principles and authorities reviewed in the judgment, including K. Kochunni v. K. Kuttanunni, to determine that the statutory criteria did not convert sthanam property into tarwad property. The majority also referred to Iswari Prosad v. N.R. Sen in discussing the meaning of the general public, while finding no evidentiary basis for public interest here.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_property_rig: A party challenged a law that restricted or removed a person’s property rights on constitutional grounds.
predicates.law_transfers_property_from_holder_to_ot: The law transferred property or a proprietary interest from its existing holder to other persons.
predicates.statutory_criteria_are_unrelated_to_prop: The law’s conditions for transferring the property did not establish, under the applicable property law, that the recipients owned it.
predicates.recipients_have_no_present_property_inte: Before the law operated, the recipients had no present proprietary interest in the property, though they might have had a contingent right of succession.
predicates.transfer_lacks_public_interest_justifica: The record did not show that the transfer had a reasonable relation to its object or was justified in the interests of the general public.

issues.definition: When a challenged property law transfers property to persons with no present interest based on criteria unrelated to title and without public-interest justification, the restriction is unreasonable and the law is invalid.

issues.legal_issue: A regional statute does not govern property outside its territorial reach unless the statute is lawfully extended to that territory.
material_facts: One petition concerned properties situated in an area that had formed part of the former Cochin State.
The Madras statute had not been extended by any legal process to that area after the reorganization of the States.
The Court left open the validity of the gift of those properties and did not decide the petitioners’ underlying property rights there.
issues.conclusion: The statute did not apply to the properties in the former Cochin area, and the petition concerning those properties was dismissed without deciding the validity of the gift or the underlying property rights.
issues.legal_principle: A legislature’s statute cannot operate extra-territorially beyond its territorial reach absent lawful extension. The Court treated the absence of an extension to the relevant area as undisputed and expressly left the gift’s validity open.

predicates.challenge_concerns_property_outside_stat: The proceeding concerns property located outside the territory to which the challenged statute applies.
predicates.statute_was_not_lawfully_extended_to_pro: No lawful measure extended the statute to the territory where the property is located.

issues.definition: If a proceeding concerns property outside a statute’s territorial scope and the statute was not lawfully extended there, the statute does not apply to that property.
